WebDAV working-directory hijack: signed binary spawns child from remote share (CVE-2025-33053) AIExploitation High
Hunts the CVE-2025-33053 technique the operator reproduced: a .url shortcut launches a legitimate signed Windows binary (e.g. iediagcmd.exe) whose working directory points at an attacker WebDAV share, so a bare-filename helper like route.exe is loaded from the remote DavWWWRoot instead of System32. Detection keys on any process whose image path resolves to a WebDAV share (DavWWWRoot / @SSL@ crumbs), which is the article's core execution primitive. Rationale: Anchors on the exact WebDAV path markers (DavWWWRoot, @SSL@) that appear in the operator's recovered README example summerartcamp[.]net@ssl@443\DavWWWRoot\OSYxaOjr and in Check Point's original Stealth Falcon writeup of CVE-2025-33053 — any executable image resolving from a WebDAV share is anomalous. Cross-checked against: • https://research.checkpoint.com/2025/stealth-falcon-zero-day/ • https://www.cisa.gov/known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog
ATT&CKT1574.008 T1204.002 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate WebDAV-mounted document shares in enterprises that publish tools over SSL WebDAV
  • Sysinternals live.sysinternals.com WebDAV usage by admins running tools directly from the share
  • SharePoint/Office WebDAV drive redirection when opening Office binaries from a mapped SSL share
  • Backup or DMS agents that stage executables on a WebDAV endpoint
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "sysinternals" and DeviceName in (dynamic([])))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull the parent process and command line — confirm a signed system binary (iediagcmd.exe, or one of the 59 candidate LOLBAS/.NET tools) launched a helper whose FolderPath is a remote DavWWWRoot/@SSL@ share; capture the WebDAV host and correlate to the C2 IOC list. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host, kill the process tree, and block the WebDAV host at proxy/firewall; disable the WebClient service via GPO on at-risk fleets. Step 3 (hunt): Sweep for .url files referencing @SSL@/DavWWWRoot, WebClient service starts, and davclnt.dll reaching external hosts across the estate.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has "DavWWWRoot" or FolderPath has "@SSL@"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has "DavWWWRoot" or NewProcessName has "@SSL@"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

search-ms: URI opening a remote WebDAV share filtered to .scr payloads AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the delivery step where the gobf[.]mx CURP lookalike page's download button fired a search-ms: query that opened the operator's WebDAV share as an Explorer search filtered to .scr files. Detection keys on process command lines combining the search-ms: protocol handler with a remote WebDAV crumb, the article's specific initial-access mechanism. Rationale: The article explicitly states the download button fired a search-ms: query opening the WebDAV share filtered to .scr files; the search-ms:+WebDAV-crumb pairing is a high-fidelity, article-specific delivery artifact rarely seen in benign use. Cross-checked against: • https://research.checkpoint.com/2025/stealth-falcon-zero-day/
ATT&CKT1204.001 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Power users invoking saved Explorer searches (.search-ms) against internal file servers
  • Legitimate enterprise WebDAV document portals accessed via search connectors
  • IT scripts building search-ms federated search connectors for SharePoint
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Extract the remote host from the search-ms crumb and confirm whether the target extension filter is .scr/.exe; check browser history for gobf[.]mx or other CURP-lookalike domains immediately prior. Step 2 (contain): Block the WebDAV host and typosquat domain; quarantine any .scr downloaded from the share. Step 3 (hunt): Look for subsequent .scr execution, Inno Setup child processes, and injection into signed Qihoo 360 (360*.exe) processes on the same host.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "search-ms:"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("DavWWWRoot", "@SSL@", "crumb")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has "search-ms:"
| where CommandLine has_any ("DavWWWRoot", "@SSL@", "crumb")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

RTLO / double-extension executable masquerading as a CURP PDF report AIDelivery High
Hunts the most-delivered lure: a .scr executable whose filename was flipped with a right-to-left override (U+202E) to read as a PDF, or padded with a double extension. Detection keys on RTLO characters and pdf/doc/jpg-to-scr/exe double extensions in file writes, the article's specific masquerading trick. Rationale: The article names the lure precisely: a .scr Inno Setup installer whose filename was RTLO-flipped to read as a PDF; U+202E plus doc-to-scr double extensions are near-zero-FP masquerading signals and match a single CURP lure that drove 97.7% of launch events.
ATT&CKT1036.002 T1036.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Rare legitimate localized filenames that contain bidirectional text control characters (Arabic/Hebrew document names)
  • Security tooling deliberately writing EICAR-style test files with double extensions
  • Archive extractors preserving mojibake filenames from foreign-language ZIPs
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Render the raw filename bytes to confirm a U+202E override or double extension, then hash the file and check against the six published payload SHA256s. Step 2 (contain): Quarantine the file, isolate the host if executed, and block the delivery WebDAV host. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on the writing process for search-ms delivery and look for the Inno Setup loader executing and hollowing into a signed Qihoo 360 process.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName matches regex @"\x{202E}" or FileName matches regex @"(?i)\.(pdf|docx?|jpe?g|png)\s*\.(scr|exe)$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName matches regex @"\x{202E}" or TargetFileName matches regex @"(?i)\.(pdf|docx?|jpe?g|png)\s*\.(scr|exe)$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Signed Ubisoft-branded binary executing from a user-writable path (DlrtyGames DLL side-load) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the DlrtyGames campaign chain where a trojanized DLL is side-loaded through a signed Ubisoft binary to drop a modular .NET RAT. Detection keys on a process whose version-info company is Ubisoft running from a user-writable directory (AppData/Downloads/Temp/ProgramData/Public), the placement pattern required for DLL side-loading. Rationale: The article names a signed Ubisoft binary side-loading a trojanized DLL to drop a .NET RAT in the DlrtyGames directory; anchoring on the Ubisoft signer company plus user-writable execution path captures the staging step. Datadog/Falcon left empty because signer-company (VersionInfo) fields are Defender/ASIM-native and not carried on stock Sysmon/FDR process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1574.002 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Ubisoft Connect / Uplay legitimate updater and game launchers that self-update into AppData
  • Portable Ubisoft game copies run from a user Downloads or Desktop folder
  • QA/dev machines running unpackaged Ubisoft builds from Temp
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("UbisoftConnect.exe", "UplayInstaller.exe", "upc.exe"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Enumerate DLLs loaded by the Ubisoft binary and flag any DLL from the same user-writable folder (side-load target) or unsigned/mismatched-company DLLs; hash both binary and DLL against the published IOCs. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host, kill the process, and block C2 addresses 77.110.127.205 / 23.94.252.228. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot to .NET RAT behavior — outbound to the campaign C2 domains and persistence writes across the fleet.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has "Ubisoft" or InitiatingProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has "Ubisoft"
| where FolderPath has_any ("AppData", "Downloads", "Temp", "ProgramData", "Public")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessFileCompany has "Ubisoft"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("AppData", "Downloads", "Temp", "ProgramData", "Public")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ActingProcessFileCompany
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Known Simba Service WebDAV campaign C2 IPs, domains and payload hashes AICommand & Control Medium
Alerts on Rapid7-published indicators for both campaign chains: connections to the C2 IPs/domains or execution/write of any of the six .NET infostealer/RAT payload hashes. Straight IOC coverage to block first, per the article's guidance. Rationale: Uses the exact Rapid7-published C2 IPs (77.110.127.205, 23.94.252.228), campaign domains (gobf.mx, onedrive.cv, google.services.ug, summerartcamp.net) and six payload SHA256 hashes; these are confirmed indicators the article directs defenders to block first. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/rapid7/Rapid7-Labs
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel scanners / sandboxes in your own estate deliberately resolving the C2 domains
  • Security researchers detonating the samples in an isolated VLAN that still ships EDR telemetry
  • Passive DNS or URL-reputation appliances pre-fetching the typosquat domain
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the connecting process and whether the source host is a sandbox/research VM vs a production endpoint; correlate to any preceding search-ms/WebDAV or RTLO .scr activity. Step 2 (contain): Block the IPs and domains at egress and quarantine any host matching a payload hash. Step 3 (hunt): Sweep for the WebDAV hijack, RTLO lures, and Ubisoft side-load UCs on any host that touched the C2, and check for Qihoo 360 process hollowing.
let C2Ips = dynamic(["77.110.127.205", "23.94.252.228"]);
let C2Domains = dynamic(["gobf.mx", "onedrive.cv", "google.services.ug", "summerartcamp.net"]);
let Payloads = dynamic(["04a8018191f2e9e76072d072a933371d9d669a42de2b2a087541cd3a653b0ba7", "e8be17a7fbef48b45f1e958b3ae5ebdfcad58808969982c431a905eefcae5268", "449d1121fa275879af22a20407aa7253ac750ac8fa7ff5691101752600d645df", "a88f5ee748e60f889d046718bfe3ddcf1c5f3cba2001cad587e8953a76bf7aa9", "51a02eccdcae0483c7cbb9796738eee6c2a13b740d30e5417cda09bf418ea93b", "82e67735cf822db8f2f759e742e5bf8c54fdbd01a4170619b9e0916e1b3f5923"]);
union
(DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in (C2Ips) or RemoteUrl has_any (C2Domains)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, Account = InitiatingProcessAccountName, Indicator = strcat(RemoteIP, " ", RemoteUrl), Proc = InitiatingProcessFileName, Detail = InitiatingProcessCommandLine),
(DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where SHA256 in (Payloads)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, Account = InitiatingProcessAccountName, Indicator = SHA256, Proc = InitiatingProcessFileName, Detail = FolderPath)
| order by Timestamp desc
let C2Ips = dynamic(["77.110.127.205", "23.94.252.228"]);
let C2Domains = dynamic(["gobf.mx", "onedrive.cv", "google.services.ug", "summerartcamp.net"]);
union
(ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr in (C2Ips)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, Indicator = DstIpAddr),
(ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has_any (C2Domains)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname = SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, Indicator = DnsQuery)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 (@DestinationIp:(77.110.127.205 OR 23.94.252.228) OR @DestinationHostname:(gobf.mx OR onedrive.cv OR google.services.ug OR summerartcamp.net))
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 RemoteAddressIP4=/^(77\.110\.127\.205|23\.94\.252\.228)$/ | groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, RemoteAddressIP4, RemotePort], function=count())

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```

    from datamodel=Web

| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["04a8018191f2e9e76072d072a933371d9d669a42de2b2a087541cd3a653b0ba7", "e8be17a7fbef48b45f1e958b3ae5ebdfcad58808969982c431a905eefcae5268", "449d1121fa275879af22a20407aa7253ac750ac8fa7ff5691101752600d645df", "a88f5ee748e60f889d046718bfe3ddcf1c5f3cba2001cad587e8953a76bf7aa9", "51a02eccdcae0483c7cbb9796738eee6c2a13b740d30e5417cda09bf418ea93b", "82e67735cf822db8f2f759e742e5bf8c54fdbd01a4170619b9e0916e1b3f5923"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

HollowGraph Malware Hides C2 and Stolen Files in Microsoft 365 Events Dated 2050

The Hacker News
2026-07-20 17 use cases 7 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

A newly discovered espionage implant has been using a hijacked Microsoft 365 calendar as its command channel, planting operator instructions and smuggling out stolen files as attachments on calendar events dated to the year 2050. Group-IB, which named the malware HollowGraph, says the approach moves tasking and stolen data through legitimate Microsoft Graph API traffic, so the activity looks

ATT&CKT1021.001 T1190 T1195.002 T1486 T1528 T1555.003 T1566
Domainscloudlanecdn.com

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] HollowGraph logAzure.txt Entra credential config drop · [LLM] New Entra client secret on Graph-capable OAuth app (HollowGraph access upkeep) · Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Application-driven M365 calendar writes (HollowGraph Graph dead-drop) · [LLM] HollowGraph DNS credential-refresh channel to cloudlanecdn.com (AAAA) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] HollowGraph far-future 2050 calendar dead-drop signatures (subject GUID / File{n}.txt) · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Application-driven M365 calendar writes (HollowGraph Graph dead-drop) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts Microsoft 365 calendar/appointment items that are created or updated by an application or service principal rather than a human, which is how HollowGraph plants tasking and uploads exfil attachments through legitimate Microsoft Graph traffic. Article-specific because it pivots on the app-principal actor performing Exchange calendar CRUD, the exact dead-drop mechanism Group-IB documented. Rationale: Group-IB's core finding is calendar events written by an app rather than a person via Graph; UserType=Application on Exchange Appointment Create/Update is the highest-fidelity behavioural signature that survives the fact that no attacker domain is contacted. Cross-checked against: • https://www.group-ib.com/blog/hollowgraph-microsoft-365/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-hollowgraph-malware-uses-microsoft-graph-for-stealthy-c2-comms/
ATT&CKT1102.002 T1071
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Microsoft Bookings / scheduling apps creating appointment items on shared mailboxes
  • Teams meeting add-ins and room-finder services writing calendar events via app permissions
  • Third-party calendar-sync SaaS (Calendly, Reclaim, Zoom) with delegated Graph Calendars.ReadWrite
  • Backup/eDiscovery tools enumerating and re-writing calendar items
  • Migration tooling (BitTitan/Quest) creating appointments during mailbox moves
Suppression filter
| where not(ClientInfoString has_any ("MicrosoftBooking","SchedulingService","Calendly","Reclaim") or AccountDisplayName has_any ("Bookings","Room Finder","Calendar Sync"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the AppId/ServicePrincipal writing the events; check if it is a sanctioned Bookings/scheduling app and whether the target mailbox normally receives app-driven calendar writes. Inspect ItemAttachments and Subject for File{n}.txt / GUID naming. Step 2 (contain): If unrecognised, revoke the app's Graph consent and disable the service principal, then reset the compromised mailbox credentials and revoke sessions. Step 3 (hunt): Enumerate every mailbox this app touched, pull all calendar items it created (esp. far-future dates), and pivot to UC covering 2050-05-13 subjects and logAzure.txt on endpoints.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where Application in ("Microsoft Exchange Online","Office 365 Exchange Online","Microsoft Graph")
| where ActionType in ("Create","Update")
| where AccountType == "Application"
| where RawEventData has_any ("Appointment","CalendarItem","IPM.Appointment")
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, Application, ApplicationId, ActionType, ObjectName, IPAddress, UserAgent, RawEventData
| order by Timestamp desc
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
| where Operation in ("Create","Update")
| where ItemType in ("Appointment","CalendarItem","Meeting")
| where UserType in ("Application","ServicePrincipal")
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, MailboxOwnerUPN, Operation, ItemType, ClientIP, ClientIPAddress, ClientInfoString, Subject, ItemAttachments
| order by TimeGenerated desc
APPLICATION
index=o365 sourcetype=o365:management:activity Workload=Exchange (Operation=Create OR Operation=Update)
| search UserType IN ("Application","ServicePrincipal") (ItemType="Appointment" OR ItemType="CalendarItem" OR ItemType="Meeting")
| stats count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(ItemType) as ItemType values(ClientIP) as ClientIP values(ClientInfoString) as ClientInfoString by UserId MailboxOwnerUPN Operation ClientAppId
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - lastTime
HollowGraph far-future 2050 calendar dead-drop signatures (subject GUID / File{n}.txt) AIActions on Objectives High
Alerts on the concrete content fingerprints of HollowGraph's dead-drop: calendar events dated 2050-05-13, subjects that are a bare GUID or match the Boss{..}ID{..} tasking scheme, and attachments named File{n}.txt. These are the exact operator artefacts Group-IB published, making this a very high-confidence, low-noise detection. Rationale: 2050-05-13, the Boss{..}ID{..} / bare-GUID subject scheme and File{n}.txt attachments are verbatim IOCs from Group-IB's report; a year-2050 calendar event carrying a File1.txt attachment has essentially no benign explanation. Cross-checked against: • https://www.group-ib.com/blog/hollowgraph-microsoft-365/ • https://www.securityweek.com/new-hollowgraph-malware-abuses-microsoft-365-calendar-for-cc-communication/
ATT&CKT1102.002 T1567
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate 'never-expire' placeholder events some scheduling tools set far in the future (rare and won't carry File{n}.txt)
  • QA/test mailboxes seeded with dummy File1.txt attachments
  • A user genuinely creating a 2050 milestone/anniversary reminder (won't have GUID subject + File{n}.txt combo)
  • Data-classification tools appending sequential FileN.txt exports to calendar bodies
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Open the flagged event; confirm the 2050-05-13 date plus GUID/Boss{}ID{} subject and File{n}.txt attachments co-occur (all three = confirmed HollowGraph). Note the app/actor that wrote it. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the affected mailbox, revoke the writing app's consent and service-principal secrets, force credential reset and session revocation. Preserve the event + attachments as evidence before deletion. Step 3 (hunt): Sweep all tenant mailboxes for far-future events and File{n}.txt attachments, and pivot to endpoints for logAzure.txt and DNS to cloudlanecdn.com to find the implant host.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where Application in ("Microsoft Exchange Online","Office 365 Exchange Online","Microsoft Graph")
| where RawEventData has "2050-05-13"
    or RawEventData matches regex @"(?i)File\d+\.txt"
    or RawEventData matches regex @"(?i)Boss\{.*\}ID\{.*\}"
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, AccountType, Application, ActionType, ObjectName, IPAddress, UserAgent, RawEventData
| order by Timestamp desc
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
| where (Subject has "2050-05-13")
    or (EventData has "2050-05-13")
    or (ItemAttachments matches regex @"(?i)File\d+\.txt")
    or (Subject matches regex @"(?i)Boss\{.*\}ID\{.*\}")
| project TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, UserId, Operation, ItemType, Subject, ItemAttachments, ClientIP, UserType
| order by TimeGenerated desc
APPLICATION
index=o365 sourcetype=o365:management:activity Workload=Exchange
| search ("2050-05-13" OR Subject="*2050-05-13*" OR Subject="*Boss{*}ID{*}*" OR "File1.txt" OR "File2.txt")
| rex field=Item.Attachments "(?<HgAttach>File\d+\.txt)"
| stats count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Subject) as Subject values(HgAttach) as HgAttach values(ClientIP) as ClientIP by MailboxOwnerUPN UserId Operation ItemType
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - lastTime
HollowGraph DNS credential-refresh channel to cloudlanecdn.com (AAAA) AICommand & Control High
Detects the cleartext DNS side-channel HollowGraph uses to refresh its Entra client-credentials, decoding tenant ID/client ID/client secret/mailbox from IPv6 AAAA records returned by cloudlanecdn[.]com. Article-specific because it anchors on the named C2 domain and the AAAA record type the malware abuses. Rationale: cloudlanecdn[.]com is a named IOC and the AAAA record type is the specific decode vector Group-IB describes; the domain has no legitimate business use, so any resolution is actionable, and scoping to AAAA further tightens fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.group-ib.com/blog/hollowgraph-microsoft-365/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-hollowgraph-malware-uses-microsoft-graph-for-stealthy-c2-comms/
ATT&CKT1071.004 T1132.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security scanners / sandboxes detonating the sample and resolving the domain during analysis
  • Threat-intel enrichment appliances proactively resolving IOC domains
  • A typo-squat/parked-domain sinkhole resolving the name for research
  • Passive-DNS collectors replaying queries
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("MsMpEng.exe","SenseIR.exe") or DeviceName has_any ("sandbox","malware-analysis"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the host and the ContextImageFileName/InitiatingProcess making the query; confirm it is not a security scanner. Frequent AAAA queries with long high-entropy subdomains under this domain = confirmed. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host, block cloudlanecdn.com at DNS/egress, and capture memory/the querying process for the .NET implant DLL. Step 3 (hunt): On the host, search for logAzure.txt and the calendar dead-drop activity; across the fleet, look for other hosts querying the same domain within the 3 Jun–9 Jul active window.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "cloudlanecdn.com"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name has "cloudlanecdn.com"
| where QueryType == 28 or QueryTypeName =~ "AAAA"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, QueryTypeName, ResultCode, ResultCodeName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

HollowGraph logAzure.txt Entra credential config drop AIInstallation High
Detects creation of logAzure.txt, the file HollowGraph disguises as a routine log to store the tenant ID, client ID, client secret and target mailbox decoded from DNS. A precise, low-noise filename IOC that flags the implant host and its stored client-credentials. Rationale: logAzure.txt is a verbatim IOC and the malware's on-disk client-credential store; an exact-filename match is high fidelity because the name is attacker-chosen and not a standard Windows/Azure log artefact. Cross-checked against: • https://www.group-ib.com/blog/hollowgraph-microsoft-365/ • https://gbhackers.com/hollowgraph-malware-turns-microsoft-365-calendar-events/
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1102
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A homegrown script or admin genuinely naming an Azure diagnostic log 'logAzure.txt'
  • Azure SDK/CLI verbose logging redirected to a similarly named file by an engineer
  • Backup software restoring an old file of that name
  • Security researcher replaying the sample in a lab host
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Azure\", @"\Microsoft SDKs\") or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("az.exe","pwsh.exe") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "-Verbose")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Read the writing process (InitiatingProcessFileName/ContextImageFileName) and file path; a non-admin process (esp. a .NET host like a rundll/dotnet loader) writing logAzure.txt is confirmed HollowGraph. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host, capture logAzure.txt and the writing binary, then rotate/revoke the Entra client secret and app credentials referenced inside it and revoke the app's Graph consent. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot from the file's parent process to the calendar dead-drop (UC1/UC2) and cloudlanecdn.com DNS (UC3), and sweep the fleet for other logAzure.txt drops.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "logAzure.txt"
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "logAzure.txt"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType
| order by TimeGenerated desc

New Entra client secret on Graph-capable OAuth app (HollowGraph access upkeep) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts newly added application/service-principal credentials in Entra ID, the mechanism HollowGraph relies on to keep its client-credentials Graph access alive. Group-IB explicitly recommends alerting on newly created client secrets for apps that can reach Graph; this surfaces credential additions for triage against the campaign. Rationale: Group-IB's identity-side guidance is to alert on newly created client secrets for Graph-capable OAuth apps; the DNS channel exists specifically to refresh those client credentials, so credential-add events are a campaign-relevant pivot even though they need enrichment for the Graph mail/calendar permission set. Cross-checked against: • https://www.group-ib.com/blog/hollowgraph-microsoft-365/ • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/hollowgraph-microsoft-calendars/
ATT&CKT1098.001
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Routine secret rotation by app owners before expiry
  • CI/CD or IaC pipelines (Terraform/Bicep) programmatically adding app credentials
  • Admins onboarding a new legitimate integration that needs Graph access
  • MSP/automation service principals rotating secrets on schedule
Suppression filter
| where Actor !endswith "$" and ActorApp !in~ ("Terraform","Azure DevOps","GitHub Actions") and Actor !has "svc-"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the target app and who added the secret; check whether the app holds Mail/Calendars Graph permissions and whether the add correlates with any anomalous sign-in or the campaign window (3 Jun–9 Jul). Step 2 (contain): For unrecognised additions, remove the new credential, disable the service principal, and review the app's granted Graph scopes and recent Graph activity. Step 3 (hunt): Correlate the app's recent mailbox/calendar operations (UC1/UC2), check for the app writing far-future events, and look for logAzure.txt / cloudlanecdn.com on endpoints tied to the actor.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("Add service principal credentials.","Update application \u2013 Certificates and secrets management","Add application credentials")
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, ActionType, ObjectName, ObjectType, IPAddress, UserAgent, RawEventData
| order by Timestamp desc
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where OperationName in ("Add service principal credentials","Update application \u2013 Certificates and secrets management","Add application credentials")
| extend Actor = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName)
| extend ActorApp = tostring(InitiatedBy.app.displayName)
| extend TargetApp = tostring(TargetResources[0].displayName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, Actor, ActorApp, TargetApp, Result, CorrelationId
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents

| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc

| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes

           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process Exploitation High

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent

OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High

Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)

| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Internet-facing devices carrying the Dropbear/Apache CVEs named in the AIVD IP-camera advisory · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Internet-facing devices carrying the Dropbear/Apache CVEs named in the AIVD IP-camera advisory AIExploitation Medium
Surfaces managed devices flagged internet-facing that carry CVE-2016-7407 (Dropbear dropbearconvert) or CVE-2021-39275 (Apache httpd < 2.4.49) — the two vulnerable services the AIVD/MIVD advisory and Censys highlighted on exposed IP cameras. This is an exposure/attack-surface hunt that operationalises the advisory's top recommendation ('find what is reachable from the public internet'), not a compromise alert. Rationale: Anchored on the only two concrete, article-named strings that survive scrutiny — CVE-2016-7407 (Dropbear dropbearconvert) and CVE-2021-39275 (Apache httpd pre-2.4.49) — pivoted on IsInternetFacing/DeviceCategory to operationalise the advisory's 'find what is exposed' guidance. The pre-extracted IP 212.187.14.204 and domain c14204.upc-c.chello.nl were dropped because no second source (AIVD brochure, The Record, SecurityAffairs) corroborated them. Cross-checked against: • https://english.aivd.nl/documents/2026/07/10/brochure-cybersecurity-advisory-russian-state-actors-are-compromising-ip-cameras • https://therecord.media/russian-intelligence-compromising-cameras-nato-ukraine-netherlands • https://securityaffairs.com/195708/intelligence/dutch-intelligence-warns-russia-uses-hacked-ip-cameras-for-military-espionage.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1078.001 T1133
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Version-banner match where the vulnerable code path isn't reachable — CVE-2021-39275 only bites when a third-party module feeds untrusted data to the affected function (the article's own caveat).
  • CVE-2016-7407 is a local malicious-key-import bug in dropbearconvert, not a remote exploit — an internet-facing hit means exposure/attack surface, not active compromise.
  • Devices flagged IsInternetFacing because of a NAT/public-IP mapping that is actually firewalled at the perimeter.
  • Patched but not yet re-scanned devices still advertising the old service banner.
  • Non-camera hosts (general web servers, NAS, VPN appliances) running the same Apache/Dropbear versions surfacing alongside the cameras you actually care about.
Suppression filter
| where DeviceCategory in~ ("NetworkDevice", "IoT") or DeviceType in~ ("Camera", "IoT", "NetworkDevice") or isnotempty(PublicIP)
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the device is genuinely reachable from the internet (test the port from an external vantage, don't trust the banner alone) and identify whether it is a camera/IoT device overlooking a logistics route, port, loading dock or other sensitive site. 2) Contain: kill the exposure — remove the port-forward/UPnP mapping, place the device behind a VPN, and rotate default/factory credentials; if the device can't support MFA or patching, pull it off the public internet entirely. 3) Hunt: pull the device's own access logs for logins or stream pulls from unrecognised IPs, and run this inventory across the whole estate to enumerate every remaining internet-facing camera so they can be locked down before an operator finds them.

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'

        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'

            - '\msedge.exe'

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
