SleeperGem loader: ruby install script spawns shell running deploy.sh AIInstallation High
Hunts the SleeperGem loader chain where a required gem spawns a child Ruby install process that executes the downloaded second-stage deploy.sh via /bin/sh. The parent-ruby → sh/deploy.sh relationship is the article-specific execution pivot common to all three trojanised gems. Rationale: deploy.sh is the named second-stage script and the process tree (ruby .../bin/install → sh -c /bin/sh '.../package/deploy.sh') is quoted verbatim in the article; requiring a ruby parent removes generic shell noise and covers all three trojanised gems. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/sleepergem-compromised-rubygems-drop-persistent-backdoor • https://www.scworld.com/brief/sleepergem-attack-targets-ruby-ecosystem-with-malicious-gems
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.004 T1497
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate gem with a native extension whose install hook happens to run a deploy.sh helper
  • Local Ruby build tooling invoking a project deploy.sh during bundle install
  • Developer manually running a script literally named deploy.sh from a Ruby wrapper
  • In-house Ruby packaging pipeline with a post-install shell step
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("git_credential_manager","Dendreo","dendreo","run_tests_firebase_testlab")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the parent ruby command line to recover the exact gem path/version; confirm it matches git_credential_manager 2.8.x, Dendreo 1.1.3/1.1.4, or the fastlane plugin 0.3.2. 2) Contain: isolate the host and terminate the ruby/sh chain before the daemon persists; snapshot the gem cache for IR. 3) Hunt: pivot to git.disroot.org egress, the ~/.local/share/gcm/ drop, and systemd/cron persistence named git-credential-manager on this and peer developer machines.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "deploy.sh"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has "ruby"
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("git_credential_manager","Dendreo","dendreo","run_tests_firebase_testlab","/bin/install")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("sh","bash","dash")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "deploy.sh" or ActingProcessCommandLine has "deploy.sh"
| where ParentProcessName has "ruby" or ActingProcessName has "ruby"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: SleeperGem gem loader executes deploy.sh via shell spawned by Ruby
id: 7d4b1e02-3a9c-4f6b-8e11-9c22ab5d7f88
description: Ruby gem install process spawns /bin/sh to run the SleeperGem second-stage deploy.sh
references:
  - https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/sleepergem-compromised-rubygems-drop-persistent-backdoor
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/21
tags:
  - attack.t1195.002
  - attack.t1059.004
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: linux
detection:
  selection:
    ParentImage|endswith: '/ruby'
    CommandLine|contains: 'deploy.sh'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE @process.command_line:*deploy.sh* AND @process.executable.path:(*/sh OR */bash OR */dash)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\/(sh|bash|dash)$/i
| CommandLine=/deploy\.sh/i
| ParentBaseFileName=/ruby/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name="sh" OR Processes.process_name="bash" OR Processes.process_name="dash") Processes.process="*deploy.sh*" Processes.parent_process_name="ruby" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name="sh" OR Processes.process_name="bash" OR Processes.process_name="dash") Processes.process="*deploy.sh*" Processes.parent_process_name="ruby" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
SleeperGem payload drop: native binary written to hidden ~/.local/share/gcm/ AIInstallation High
Hunts creation of the SleeperGem native daemon binary named git-credential-manager inside the hidden ~/.local/share/gcm/ directory, copied there by the deploy.sh stage. The exact filename+hidden-path combination is a direct host IOC from the article's cleanup guidance. Rationale: The article and remediation guidance explicitly name ~/.local/share/gcm/git-credential-manager as the dropped daemon path; the hidden directory + binary masquerading as the legitimate Microsoft tool makes this near-zero-FP on developer endpoints. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/sleepergem-compromised-rubygems-drop-persistent-backdoor • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/sleepergem-uses-three-malicious.html
ATT&CKT1105 T1036.005 T1564.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A user manually building the genuine Microsoft Git Credential Manager from source into a custom ~/.local path (uncommon; real GCM installs to /usr/local/bin or /usr/bin)
  • Backup/restore tooling recreating a previously-infected home directory
  • Dotfile sync tools replaying an old gcm artifact
  • EDR test/replay of the sample during validation
Response runbook
1) Triage: hash the dropped binary and confirm it is not the signed Microsoft GCM; capture the creating process (should trace back to deploy.sh/sh). 2) Contain: kill any running git-credential-manager --daemon, delete ~/.local/share/gcm/, and isolate the host. 3) Hunt: remove the systemd user unit and cron entry named git-credential-manager, inspect /usr/local/sbin/ping6 for a setuid shell, and rotate all reachable secrets (SSH keys, cloud creds, tokens).
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has "/.local/share/gcm/"
| where FileName == "git-credential-manager"
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath has "/.local/share/gcm/"
| where TargetFileName == "git-credential-manager"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SleeperGem persistence: git-credential-manager daemon installs systemd + cron AIInstallation High
Hunts the dropped SleeperGem binary launching itself as a background daemon and registering dual persistence via its own 'install --method=systemd|cron --service-name=git-credential-manager' subcommands. The self-install flags are exact strings from the recorded process tree. Rationale: The install subcommands '--method=systemd --service-name=git-credential-manager', '--method=cron', and '--daemon' are quoted verbatim from Harden-Runner's process capture and are anchored to the malicious ~/.local/share/gcm/ image path, distinguishing this from the real GCM which never self-installs a systemd/cron persistence pair. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/sleepergem-compromised-rubygems-drop-persistent-backdoor • https://www.developer-tech.com/news/sleepergem-rubygems-attack-evades-ci-to-hit-developer-laptops/
ATT&CKT1543.002 T1053.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine credential-manager tooling installing a user service (real GCM does not use these flags or this path)
  • Sysadmin scripting a legitimately-named git-credential-manager service for internal tooling
  • EDR replay/validation of the SleeperGem sample
  • Configuration-management run re-applying a stale service definition
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath has "/.local/share/gcm/" or ProcessCommandLine has "/.local/share/gcm/"
Response runbook
1) Triage: enumerate `systemctl --user list-units | grep git-credential-manager` and the user crontab; confirm the ExecStart/cron command points at ~/.local/share/gcm/. 2) Contain: `systemctl --user disable --now git-credential-manager`, remove the cron entry, kill the daemon, delete the drop directory. 3) Hunt: check whether the sudo/wheel escalation branch fired (getent group probes) and whether /usr/local/sbin/ping6 exists as a setuid shell; rotate every secret on the host.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "git-credential-manager"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--method=systemd","--method=cron","--daemon")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "--service-name=git-credential-manager" or ProcessCommandLine has "--daemon"
| where FolderPath has "/.local/share/gcm/" or ProcessCommandLine has "/.local/share/gcm/"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "git-credential-manager"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("--method=systemd","--method=cron","--daemon")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "/.local/share/gcm/" or TargetProcessCommandLine has "--service-name=git-credential-manager"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SleeperGem privilege escalation: setuid-root shell planted as /usr/local/sbin/ping6 AIInstallation High
Hunts creation of a file named ping6 in /usr/local/sbin, where SleeperGem's root branch plants a setuid-root copy of the system shell masquerading as a networking utility. The real ping6 ships in /bin or /usr/bin, so a ping6 in /usr/local/sbin is an unambiguous backdoor IOC. Rationale: The remediation guidance names /usr/local/sbin/ping6 as the setuid-root shell location; a ping6 binary in /usr/local/sbin (vs the distro path /bin|/usr/bin) is an extremely low-FP host IOC that catches the privilege-escalation branch even when C2 and drop are missed. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/sleepergem-compromised-rubygems-drop-persistent-backdoor • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/sleepergem-uses-three-malicious.html
ATT&CKT1548.001 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A local admin manually installing a custom iputils/ping6 build into /usr/local/sbin (rare)
  • Configuration management deploying a legitimately-compiled ping6 to /usr/local/sbin
  • Backup restore recreating a previously-infected sbin
  • EDR replay/validation of the SleeperGem sample
Response runbook
1) Triage: `ls -l /usr/local/sbin/ping6` and check for the setuid bit (`-rwsr-xr-x`) and whether the file is actually a shell (`file`/strings); confirm it is not a genuine iputils build. 2) Contain: remove the setuid file, isolate the host, and treat it as root-compromised. 3) Hunt: review who could run passwordless sudo, audit the daemon's getent group sudo/wheel probes, and rotate all root-reachable secrets and any credentials the native daemon could have harvested.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath == "/usr/local/sbin" and FileName == "ping6"
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath == "/usr/local/sbin/ping6"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")

   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"

            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'

            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'

UAC-0145 Uses ClickFix CAPTCHAs to Infect Ukrainian Devices wih Malware

The Hacker News
2026-07-19 17 use cases 9 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Russian state-sponsored threat actors have been observed leveraging the infamous ClickFix strategy to trick Ukrainian targets into infecting their own machines with data-stealing malware. According to the Computer Emergency Response Team of Ukraine (CERT-UA), the activity has been attributed to UAC-0145, a sub-cluster within Sandworm, an advanced hacking unit affiliated with GRU, Russia's

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] UAC-0145 ClickFix: explorer-spawned PowerShell downloads + drops VBS to Startup (GHETTOVIBE) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] GHETTOVIBE persistence: VBS written to Startup folder by script host / PowerShell · Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] UAC-0145 ClickFix C2 / staging domain contact (office366.com, 365softupdate.com, delta.smartlinkupload.com) · [LLM] EtherHiding: browser fetching UAC-0145 C2 domain from Ethereum/BSC smart contract via public RPC · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
UAC-0145 ClickFix: explorer-spawned PowerShell downloads + drops VBS to Startup (GHETTOVIBE) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the ClickFix execution step where a victim pastes the fake-CAPTCHA command into the Run dialog, causing explorer.exe to spawn PowerShell/cmd that both fetches a remote payload and writes a VBS autorun into the Startup directory. Article-specific: the GHETTOVIBE variant is delivered exactly this way (download + save VBS to Startup). Rationale: Ties the exact GHETTOVIBE delivery chain from the article — a pasted ClickFix command (parent explorer.exe from Win+R) that downloads AND writes a VBS to Startup — into one process event, avoiding the generic 'browser click + exec' rule already deployed. Cross-checked against: • https://socprime.com/active-threats/primary-compromise-vectors-used-by-uac-0145-as-of-july-2026/ • https://therecord.media/ukraine-sandworm-hacks-captcha-powershell • https://www.bitdefender.com/en-us/blog/hotforsecurity/ukraine-fake-captchas-hack-yourself
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001 T1547.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sysadmin manually pasting a legitimate install one-liner into the Run box that fetches and installs software
  • Software-deployment tooling that stages a helper script into the Startup folder
  • Login-script or GPO troubleshooting where an admin writes a .vbs autorun by hand
  • Browser/self-service portals that legitimately invoke certutil for cert enrollment then touch Startup
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("chocolatey","winget","C:\\ProgramData\\chocolatey") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full ProcessCommandLine and resolve the download URL/host; check whether the fetched file is a .vbs and whether it landed in the per-user Startup path. Confirm the initiating user actually used Win+R (session/interactive context). 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the PowerShell/wscript tree, delete the dropped VBS from Startup, and block the download domain at proxy/DNS. 3) Hunt: sweep for the same URL/VBS hash org-wide, look for follow-on SCOUTCURL recon (PowerShell system enumeration) and connections to office366.com / 365softupdate.com / delta.smartlinkupload.com.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "explorer.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Invoke-WebRequest","iwr ","DownloadString","DownloadFile","Start-BitsTransfer","curl ","certutil")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Startup",@"\Start Menu\Programs\Startup",".vbs")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\explorer.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\powershell.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\pwsh.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\cmd.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\mshta.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any ("Invoke-WebRequest","iwr ","DownloadString","DownloadFile","Start-BitsTransfer","curl ","certutil")
| where CommandLine has_any ("Startup","\\Start Menu\\Programs\\Startup",".vbs")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: UAC-0145 ClickFix PowerShell From Run Dialog Downloading VBS To Startup

logsource:

detection:

source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\\explorer.exe OR *\\Explorer.EXE) @Image:(*\\powershell.exe OR *\\PowerShell.exe OR *\\cmd.exe OR *\\mshta.exe OR *\\MSHTA.EXE) @CommandLine:(*Invoke-WebRequest* OR *iwr* OR *DownloadString* OR *DownloadFile* OR *Start-BitsTransfer* OR *certutil*) AND @CommandLine:(*Startup* OR *.vbs*)

| CommandLine=/(Invoke-WebRequest|iwr\s|DownloadString|DownloadFile|Start-BitsTransfer|certutil)/i

GHETTOVIBE persistence: VBS written to Startup folder by script host / PowerShell AIInstallation High
Hunts the persistence artifact of UAC-0145's ClickFix chain: a .vbs file created directly in the Startup autorun directory by powershell, cmd, wscript/cscript or mshta. This is the on-disk footprint of the GHETTOVIBE autorun, independent of how the command was launched. Rationale: A .vbs created in the Startup folder by an interpreter is a rare, high-fidelity persistence artifact and is exactly the GHETTOVIBE behaviour CERT-UA described; catches the campaign even when the launching command line is obfuscated or not captured.
ATT&CKT1547.001 T1059.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legacy line-of-business apps that self-install a VBS logon helper into Startup on first run
  • IT logon-automation scripts (mapped drives, printer setup) deployed as Startup VBS
  • Software packagers/MSI custom actions dropping a VBS shim
  • User-created troubleshooting scripts placed in Startup by an admin
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "gpscript" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Program Files"
Response runbook
1) Triage: hash the VBS and read its contents (deobfuscate); confirm the writing process and account, and check for a preceding explorer.exe→PowerShell download in the same session. 2) Contain: isolate the host, remove the VBS, and disable the autorun; capture the file for analysis. 3) Hunt: search the org for the same VBS hash/name, correlate with SCOUTCURL recon and beacons to the campaign domains, and check for the loaders FLUIDLEECH/LOADLOOP masquerading as antivirus tools.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FileName endswith ".vbs"
| where FolderPath has @"\Start Menu\Programs\Startup"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFileName endswith ".vbs"
| where TargetFilePath has "\\Start Menu\\Programs\\Startup"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

UAC-0145 ClickFix C2 / staging domain contact (office366.com, 365softupdate.com, delta.smartlinkupload.com) AICommand & Control High
Alerts on any endpoint resolving or connecting to the named UAC-0145 delivery/C2 domains from the ClickFix campaign. These domains were corroborated across CERT-UA, SOC Prime and the article's pre-extracted IOC set and are not legitimate infrastructure. Rationale: Direct, second-source-confirmed IOC domains (CERT-UA + SOC Prime + article) — exact-match network/DNS hits are the highest-fidelity signal available for this campaign and warrant alerting rather than hunting. Cross-checked against: • https://socprime.com/active-threats/primary-compromise-vectors-used-by-uac-0145-as-of-july-2026/ • https://thecyberexpress.com/clickfix-attacks-fuel-uac-0145-cyber-campaigns/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1568
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A security researcher/analyst detonating the sample intentionally in the same tenant
  • Typo-squat confusion where a user meant office365.com and mistyped — still worth reviewing
  • Threat-intel/proxy sandbox appliance pre-fetching the URL for enrichment
  • cloaking.house appearing because a marketer legitimately trialled the Cloaking.House SaaS from a corporate host
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process and user; a browser hit suggests visiting a compromised site, a script-host/PowerShell hit suggests active C2/staging. 2) Contain: sinkhole/block the domains at DNS and proxy, isolate any host with a non-browser initiating process. 3) Hunt: for confirmed hosts, look back for the ClickFix PowerShell drop, VBS-in-Startup persistence, SCOUTCURL recon, and outbound Dropbox API / steamcommunity.com dead-drop traffic used by the same actor.

| order by Timestamp desc

| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DvcHostname, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

EtherHiding: browser fetching UAC-0145 C2 domain from Ethereum/BSC smart contract via public RPC AICommand & Control Low
Hunts the SMARTAXE/EtherHiding step where injected CAPTCHA JavaScript in the victim's browser queries a public Ethereum/BSC RPC endpoint to resolve the next-stage C2 domain from a smart contract. Flags browsers making connections to public blockchain RPC providers — an abnormal pattern for most enterprise endpoints. Rationale: Targets the article's distinctive EtherHiding/SMARTAXE mechanism (C2 domain pulled from an Ethereum smart contract) via the observable side-effect: a browser hitting a public blockchain RPC. High FP in crypto-using orgs, so scoped as hunting with first-seen aggregation. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/dprk-adopts-etherhiding • https://www.elastic.co/docs/reference/security/prebuilt-rules/rules/macos/command_and_control_potential_etherhiding_c2
ATT&CKT1568 T1102 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Employees legitimately using crypto/web3 sites, wallets or NFT marketplaces from managed browsers
  • Browser extensions (MetaMask etc.) periodically polling RPC endpoints
  • Developers testing dApps against Infura/Ankr/BSC public nodes
  • Ad/analytics scripts that embed web3 wallet-connect libraries on benign sites
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "--utility-sub-type" and DeviceName !in (dynamic([]))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the referring website (browser history/proxy) that triggered the RPC call and check whether it is a known-good crypto app or an unexpected/compromised site presenting a CAPTCHA; suppress hosts with sanctioned wallet extensions. 2) Contain: if the referrer is a compromised/unknown site, block it and the RPC endpoint at proxy, and isolate if a PowerShell/VBS chain follows. 3) Hunt: correlate the same device for a subsequent ClickFix PowerShell run, VBS-in-Startup persistence, and beacons to office366.com / 365softupdate.com / delta.smartlinkupload.com.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe","arc.exe")
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("bsc-dataseed","cloudflare-eth.com","mainnet.infura.io","rpc.ankr.com","eth.llamarpc.com","bscrpc.com","binance.org","nodereal.io","quiknode.pro")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), Hits=count(), Endpoints=make_set(RemoteUrl, 20) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has_any ("bsc-dataseed","cloudflare-eth.com","mainnet.infura.io","rpc.ankr.com","eth.llamarpc.com","bscrpc.com","binance.org","nodereal.io","quiknode.pro")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), Hits=count(), Domains=make_set(DnsQuery, 20) by SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DvcHostname
| order by FirstSeen desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user

    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High

          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SonicWall SMA Zero-Days Exploited Before Disclosure to Gain Root Access

The Hacker News
2026-07-19 19 use cases 7 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A previously undocumented threat actor has been attributed to the exploitation of recently disclosed SonicWall Secure Mobile Access (SMA) 1000 series VPN appliances as zero-days prior their public disclosure since June 22, 2026. Cybersecurity company Volexity is tracking the activity under the moniker UTA0533. The discovery was made following an incident response investigation earlier this

Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] SonicWall SMA tcpdump LDAP credential sniffing via lib.sh (UTA0533) · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
SonicWall SMA pre-auth /wsproxy WebSocket bypass (CVE-2026-15409) via 'SMA Connect Agent' UA + bmID=-3389 AIExploitation High
Hunts the unauthenticated CVE-2026-15409 entry request UTA0533 used to open a WebSocket tunnel to localhost-only services on SonicWall SMA 1000 appliances. The signature is a request to /wsproxy carrying User-Agent 'SMA Connect Agent' and a URI parameter bmID beginning with -3389 — the exact magic values Volexity documented. Rationale: Uses the two article-specific magic values Volexity published: User-Agent 'SMA Connect Agent' plus URI parameter bmID starting with -3389 on /wsproxy — a fingerprint no legitimate client emits, making this a near-zero-FP pre-auth exploit signature. Cross-checked with Volexity and Rapid7 write-ups. Cross-checked against: • https://www.volexity.com/blog/2026/07/17/proxying-to-compromise-sonicwall-secure-mobile-access-0-day-exploitation/ • https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/etr-rapid7-mdr-team-discovers-new-sonicwall-sma1000-zero-days-being-actively-exploited-cve-2026-15409-cve-2026-15410/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/sonicwall-sma1000-flaws-exploited-as-zero-days-to-push-custom-malware/
ATT&CKT1190 T1133
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized vulnerability scanners (Tenable/Rapid7/Nessus) replaying the CVE-2026-15409 PoC against the appliance
  • Internal red-team / pentest engagement reproducing the exploit chain
  • SonicWall support running diagnostic reproduction of the flaw
  • Security researchers mass-scanning internet-facing SMA appliances post-disclosure
Response runbook
1. Triage: Pull the full request/response for the matching /wsproxy hit and the source IP; confirm the bmID=-3389 parameter and 'SMA Connect Agent' UA, and check whether the WebSocket upgrade succeeded (HTTP 101). Cross-reference the source IP against the campaign IOC IPs (108.205.8.173, 147.45.51.19, 150.241.210.53, 202.8.105.201, 217.77.15.99, 42.200.172.14, 81.19.140.217, 89.117.20.1). 2. Contain: If not an authorized test, block the source IP at the perimeter, take the appliance offline or restrict management access, and confirm the SMA 1000 firmware is patched for CVE-2026-15409/15410. 3. Hunt: On the appliance inspect /tmp, /var/tmp for staged files (hypdate.b64), /usr/bin/xzfind, deploy_new.py, and review /var/lib/unit/conf.json and /etc/init.d/workplace for attacker routes/persistence.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has "/wsproxy"
| where HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent has "SMA Connect Agent"
| where Url has "bmID=-3389"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstHostname, HttpMethod, Url, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, HttpStatusCode
| order by TimeGenerated desc

UTA0533 ORANGETAIL/Suo5 web shell access on SonicWall SMA (/workplace/error.jsp, /workplace/dialogs/errorDialog.jsp) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts requests to the two attacker-registered JSP routes that KNUCKLEBALL wired into the SMA appliance to reach the Suo5 HTTP proxy and the ORANGETAIL Behinder-like Java web shell. These decoy 'error' paths are how UTA0533 interacts with its implants over internet-accessible URIs. Rationale: Pins on the two exact URI paths Volexity attributes to the Suo5 and ORANGETAIL routes injected by KNUCKLEBALL. POST method and request volume separate web-shell tasking from the rare genuine error-page GET, keeping this deployable despite the decoy naming. Cross-checked against: • https://www.volexity.com/blog/2026/07/17/proxying-to-compromise-sonicwall-secure-mobile-access-0-day-exploitation/ • https://gbhackers.com/hackers-exploit-sonicwall-sma-zero-days-to-gain-root-access/
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1071.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine users hitting the legitimate SonicWall workplace error.jsp page after a portal error (GET, low volume)
  • Uptime/health-check monitors polling a workplace error page
  • Vulnerability scanners crawling the appliance and touching every JSP path
  • Load balancer synthetic transactions probing known SMA endpoints
Suppression filter
| where http_method="POST" OR count > 5
Response runbook
1. Triage: Isolate POST requests and high-volume hits to the two JSP paths; capture request bodies (ORANGETAIL sends encrypted Java payloads) and the source IPs, and correlate against the /wsproxy exploit hits from UC1 on the same appliance. 2. Contain: Block offending source IPs, and on the appliance kill the injected NGINX Unit routes in /var/lib/unit/conf.json and remove the Suo5 (agent_wp8.jar) / ORANGETAIL (agent_wp9.jar) payloads and deploy_new.py. 3. Hunt: Review appliance memory and processes for the injected JARs, check for credential/session-DB and TOTP seed access, and pivot on any internal hosts the Suo5 proxy tunneled to.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has_any ("/workplace/error.jsp", "/workplace/dialogs/errorDialog.jsp")
| summarize Requests=count(), Methods=make_set(HttpMethod), UserAgents=make_set(HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated) by SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, Url
| where Methods has "POST" or Requests > 5   // 5 = tolerate occasional genuine error-page GETs; POST or volume = web-shell interaction
| order by LastSeen desc

SonicWall SMA appliance implant & persistence artifacts (ROOTRUN xzfind, KNUCKLEBALL deploy_new.py, init.d/workplace, Unit conf.json) AIInstallation High
Hunts creation or modification of the on-disk artifacts UTA0533 dropped on SonicWall SMA appliances: the setuid ROOTRUN binary /usr/bin/xzfind, the KNUCKLEBALL dropper deploy_new.py, the CVE-2026-15410 exploit stager /tmp/hypdate.b64, the LDAP-sniffer /var/tmp/lib.sh, and tampering of /etc/init.d/workplace and /var/lib/unit/conf.json for persistence and route injection. Rationale: Every path is a concrete IOC named by Volexity and echoed by BleepingComputer (xzfind/ROOTRUN, deploy_new.py/KNUCKLEBALL, hypdate.b64, lib.sh, conf.json route injection, init.d/workplace persistence); appliance filesystem paths like /var/lib/unit/conf.json and /usr/lib/python3.11/site-packages are unique enough to make file-touch events high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.volexity.com/blog/2026/07/17/proxying-to-compromise-sonicwall-secure-mobile-access-0-day-exploitation/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/sonicwall-sma1000-flaws-exploited-as-zero-days-to-push-custom-malware/
ATT&CKT1037.004 T1548.001 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SonicWall firmware update or hotfix legitimately rewriting /var/lib/unit/conf.json or /etc/init.d/workplace
  • Administrator troubleshooting scripts placed in /var/tmp
  • Vendor support bundle collection touching appliance system paths
  • Backup/restore of appliance configuration overwriting init.d or Unit config
Response runbook
1. Triage: Identify which artifact fired and the writing process/user context — note that Volexity found /tmp files owned by the appliance's unprivileged database (couchdb) account, so a non-root writer of these paths is itself a strong signal. Confirm whether /usr/bin/xzfind has the setuid bit. 2. Contain: Take the appliance offline, preserve /tmp, /var/tmp, deploy_new.py, and conf.json for forensics, then rebuild/re-image from a known-good SonicWall image rather than deleting files in place (memory-resident implants survive file removal). 3. Hunt: Diff /var/lib/unit/conf.json and /etc/init.d/workplace against a clean baseline to enumerate injected routes, and search other appliances in the fleet for the same paths and for the /wsproxy exploit hits from UC1.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("/usr/bin/xzfind", "deploy_new.py", "/tmp/hypdate.b64", "/var/tmp/lib.sh", "/etc/init.d/workplace", "/var/lib/unit/conf.json")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostIP, Facility, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SonicWall SMA tcpdump LDAP credential sniffing via lib.sh (UTA0533) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts UTA0533's post-root credential harvesting on the SMA appliance: the /var/tmp/lib.sh helper launching tcpdump to capture unencrypted LDAP (port 389) traffic and extract usernames and passwords processed by the appliance. Packet capture of LDAP on a VPN appliance is not normal operations. Rationale: Combines the article's named helper /var/tmp/lib.sh with tcpdump filtering on LDAP/389 — the exact credential-capture behaviour Volexity described; tcpdump sniffing cleartext LDAP on a gateway appliance is rare enough that the LDAP/389 qualifier makes it alertable. Cross-checked against: • https://www.volexity.com/blog/2026/07/17/proxying-to-compromise-sonicwall-secure-mobile-access-0-day-exploitation/ • https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/etr-rapid7-mdr-team-discovers-new-sonicwall-sma1000-zero-days-being-actively-exploited-cve-2026-15409-cve-2026-15410/
ATT&CKT1040 T1552.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Administrator running an authorized packet capture to troubleshoot LDAP/AD authentication on the appliance
  • SonicWall support diagnostic capture during a support case
  • Network monitoring/NDR tooling legitimately capturing traffic on the appliance
  • Scheduled diagnostic scripts that invoke tcpdump for health checks
Response runbook
1. Triage: Identify the parent process (expect /var/tmp/lib.sh or a shell spawned from the compromised service account, not an admin session) and the tcpdump capture filter/output file; if the parent is lib.sh or the couchdb/db service account, treat as confirmed. 2. Contain: Kill the tcpdump process, capture and remove /var/tmp/lib.sh and any .pcap output for forensics, take the appliance offline and rotate all credentials and TOTP seeds that transit it (LDAP bind accounts, VPN user creds, session tokens). 3. Hunt: Correlate with UC1/UC3 on the same appliance to confirm the full chain, and review LDAP/AD logs and downstream systems for use of any credentials that may have been captured before containment.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where SyslogMessage has "tcpdump"
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("389", "ldap", "lib.sh")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostIP, Facility, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:

            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'

            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'

falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

        "Add OAuth2PermissionGrant",

    by Authentication.user, Authentication.app, Authentication.src, Authentication.signature
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1003.001
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:
            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'
            - '\SearchProtocolHost.exe'
    condition: selection and not filter_known_good
falsepositives:
    - Third-party EDR / forensic tools — extend the filter list
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High

status: experimental
description: |

    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when

    vendor.
references:

            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("81a9af3846bad3a1107164ff7cf0a08e020b31a3b32fd17866e17d4c1565f7f2", "8c470301dcb7278f73e622f1950073567b34011c64b60cdfbb0f89803923a5a3", "1e1e68bbb899450a57274a8b12082ed4e2040a2aae77014f20431689d2b4edee", "ea9154e374e4f77bc2cf54282e23543573980342a85bc888cb23f20b8bbba081", "04d4a9fbb32e967200eb98be014ca914a03bfa6b", "b4ee1f50fbb49f0ff5fde3d026343bc23ee08d51", "c2b0ae0a1f42a139abe4dd612676066ec1426394", "5e5b716f2385c818ec61198be1a2a07a4560eac5", "5cb00bbfe818ee3e85fb99ab1db1af7c", "b6df166291f80ee89032d769c99714f3", "54d21399b8b52b48a0fef68450593e45", "5f3a55201c511c9ff9be4c16c41028a2") or SHA1 in~ ("81a9af3846bad3a1107164ff7cf0a08e020b31a3b32fd17866e17d4c1565f7f2", "8c470301dcb7278f73e622f1950073567b34011c64b60cdfbb0f89803923a5a3", "1e1e68bbb899450a57274a8b12082ed4e2040a2aae77014f20431689d2b4edee", "ea9154e374e4f77bc2cf54282e23543573980342a85bc888cb23f20b8bbba081", "04d4a9fbb32e967200eb98be014ca914a03bfa6b", "b4ee1f50fbb49f0ff5fde3d026343bc23ee08d51", "c2b0ae0a1f42a139abe4dd612676066ec1426394", "5e5b716f2385c818ec61198be1a2a07a4560eac5", "5cb00bbfe818ee3e85fb99ab1db1af7c", "b6df166291f80ee89032d769c99714f3", "54d21399b8b52b48a0fef68450593e45", "5f3a55201c511c9ff9be4c16c41028a2") or MD5 in~ ("81a9af3846bad3a1107164ff7cf0a08e020b31a3b32fd17866e17d4c1565f7f2", "8c470301dcb7278f73e622f1950073567b34011c64b60cdfbb0f89803923a5a3", "1e1e68bbb899450a57274a8b12082ed4e2040a2aae77014f20431689d2b4edee", "ea9154e374e4f77bc2cf54282e23543573980342a85bc888cb23f20b8bbba081", "04d4a9fbb32e967200eb98be014ca914a03bfa6b", "b4ee1f50fbb49f0ff5fde3d026343bc23ee08d51", "c2b0ae0a1f42a139abe4dd612676066ec1426394", "5e5b716f2385c818ec61198be1a2a07a4560eac5", "5cb00bbfe818ee3e85fb99ab1db1af7c", "b6df166291f80ee89032d769c99714f3", "54d21399b8b52b48a0fef68450593e45", "5f3a55201c511c9ff9be4c16c41028a2")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
